newsitem.title: INDIA: Germany says India's nuclear stance hurts U.N. bid.
newsitem.headline: Germany says India's nuclear stance hurts U.N. bid.

text.p: Germany on Friday backed India's drive to become a permanent member of the United Nations Security Council, but said New Delhi's opposition to a global nuclear test ban pact had set back its chances.
"We think India is entitled to claim a permanent seat and so India is a candidate whom we support," visiting German Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel told a news conference in the Indian capital.
Kinkel, who is Germany's second-highest official after Chancellor Helmut Kohl, said India's U.N. campaign has been hampered by its firm opposition to the Comprehensive Test Ban Treaty (CTBT).
The Security Council currently has five permanent members -- the United States, China, France, Britain and Russia. Both Germany and India are pushing to become permanent members.
Kinkel said that in talks with Indian leaders on Thursday he tried to point out the relationship between the CTBT and India's bid to become a permanent member of the Security Council.
"There is some connection," Kinkel said through an interpreter. "It would be wrong to deny that some connection does exist."
Kinkel noted that last year India fell far short in its bid to be elected to one of the rotating non-permanent Security Council seats after New Delhi rejected the CTBT.
Indian Foreign Minister Inder Kumar Gujral, speaking at the same news conference, reiterated New Delhi's strong opposition to the CTBT, which has been signed by almost 140 nations.
"India will not sign the CTBT, either now or later," he said. "India is in favour of the abolition of nuclear weapons, but the CTBT is neither comprehensive nor would it ban tests."

India, which stood in near isolation against the treaty while it was negotiated last year, claims it would allow the five declared nuclear powers -- the United States, Russia, China, France and Britain -- to continue laboratory tests.
New Delhi has insisted that the nuclear powers agree to commit to a timetable for nuclear disarmament.
Kinkel, who was on the second day of a three-day visit, said he had urged the Indian government to press ahead with economic reforms and to open up its financial and insurance sectors.
A list of projects proposed by German businesses was presented to New Delhi, underlining Germany's strong interest in investing in the South Asian nation's infrastructure sector, Kinkel said.
